steps.say: Shock wave lithotripsy is best for small soft stones outside the lower pole of the kidney. Stones under 20 mm with attenuation below 1000 Hounsfield units on CT are ideal. A stone in the lowest cup clears poorly because fragments must float uphill. Hard brushite and cystine stones are resistant to shock waves even at ideal size. Always check the CT density and composition clues before booking the machine.
steps.tx: **Shock wave lithotripsy** (stone breaking with focused sound waves) clears **renal calculi** (kidney stones) best when the stone sits outside the **lower pole** (lowest kidney cup), measures under **20 mm** (two centimetres), and shows attenuation below 1000 HU (Hounsfield units, soft on the CT density scale). Hard brushite or cystine stones resist fragmentation even at ideal size, so check composition clues before booking the ESWL (shock wave treatment) machine.

vis.alt: Illustration of a kidney stone fragmenting under shock waves, with staghorn stone, ureteric stone, laser and basket panels.
vis.caption: Shock waves fragment the renal stone: choose shock wave lithotripsy for stones under 20 mm outside the lower pole. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Shock wave lithotripsy is forbidden in pregnancy and in uncorrected bleeding disorders. An active untreated urinary infection must be sterilised first. Severe skeletal deformity is also a bar, because positioning will fail. Correct coagulation and clear the urine before booking. Fragment passage through an infected system can trigger life threatening urosepsis.
steps.tx: Four absolute bars stop **ESWL** (shock wave stone treatment): **pregnancy** (unborn child at risk), uncorrected **bleeding diathesis** (clotting failure that bleeds around the kidney), active untreated urinary infection (germ load that seeds the blood), and severe skeletal malformation (deformed spine that blocks positioning). Sterilise the urine and correct coagulation first, because fragment passage after shock waves can precipitate urosepsis in an infected system.

rows: Shock waves and X-rays endanger the foetus

steps.say: Steinstrasse is German for stone street. It describes a column of fragments blocking the ureter after shock wave treatment. Most columns are passed on their own with pain relief and fluids. A JJ stent is placed or ureteroscopy is performed when fever appears. Persistent blockage and solitary kidneys are indications for drainage. Stagnant infected urine above the column can progress rapidly to sepsis.
steps.tx: **Steinstrasse** (stone street, a column of chips) forms when ESWL fragments stack in the **ureter** (urine tube to the bladder) and block flow. Most columns pass with conservative care and analgesia. Intervene with a **JJ stent** (internal double J splint) or **ureteroscopy** (telescope clearance) when fever, persistent obstruction, or a solitary kidney threatens function, because stagnant infected urine above the column rapidly progresses to urosepsis.

vis.alt: Illustration of a ureteric calculus blocking the ureter with hydronephrosis and hydroureter above it.
vis.caption: A ureteric stone blocks drainage: fragment columns stack the same way as steinstrasse, relieved by stent or ureteroscopy. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The Holmium YAG laser is the workhorse of modern ureteroscopy. It delivers light at 2100 nanometres, heating water inside stone pores. Energy penetrates only 0.4 mm into surrounding fluid, so the ureter wall stays safe. It breaks every stone type, including cystine and hard calcium oxalate. The fibre tip is kept away from tissue and firing stays in short bursts. Prolonged firing in a tight calyx can scald the lining.
steps.tx: The **Holmium:YAG laser** (2100 nm light scalpel) vaporises stones by a **photothermal mechanism** (heat from absorbed light) with absorption depth of only **0.4 mm** (shallow safety margin). It fragments every composition, including hard calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine that defeat shock waves. Keep the fibre tip one millimetre from the urothelium and fire in short bursts, because continuous firing in a narrow calyx heats irrigant and injures mucosa.

steps.say: The thulium fiber laser is tuned to 1940 nanometres, closer to the water absorption peak. Stones are turned into fine dust with minimal kickback toward the kidney. Its slim fibres are flexible and lower pole deflection is preserved. Irrigation is improved around the thinner fibre profile. Dust washes out on its own, while larger chunks still need basket removal. Dusting mode is selected for bulky kidney stones.
steps.tx: The **thulium fiber laser** (TFL (fine fibre laser), a dusting tool on a glass fibre) sits nearer the water absorption peak, so it produces finer dust with less **retropulsion** (backward stone kick). Slim fibres (**150 micrometres** to 200 micrometres, hair thin) preserve scope deflection into the lower pole and improve irrigant flow. Choose dusting settings for large renal stones and fragmentation settings for hard ureteric stones, because dust washes out spontaneously while chunks need basket extraction.

steps.say: A ureteral access sheath is a hollow tube that straightens the ureter. Common sizes are 10/12F and 12/14F French calibre. Irrigation fluid is vented and kidney pressure is kept below 30 cmH2O. Low pressure stops irrigant from entering veins and reduces sepsis after long laser sessions. The ureter is often swollen mildly after sheath use. A stent is left whenever the lining looks grazed.
steps.tx: A **ureteral access sheath** (hollow working channel) in **10/12F or 12/14F** (French calibre pair) straightens the ureter and vents irrigant, holding **intrarenal pressure** (fluid pressure inside the kidney) below **30 cmH2O** (safe pressure ceiling). Low pressure blocks pyelovenous backflow (irrigant reflux into veins) and cuts postoperative sepsis after long lasing. Expect mild ureteric wall oedema after sheath cases and leave a stent when mucosa looks grazed, because an oedematous ureter obstructs silently overnight.

steps.say: Stones in the lowest cup of the kidney are cleared poorly after shock waves. Fragments must float uphill against gravity through a narrow neck. An entry angle below 30 degrees is a trap for every chip. A tunnel longer than 30 mm or narrower than 5 mm is also blocked. Such kidneys are sent directly for flexible ureteroscopy. The deflectable laser fibre is used where shock wave fragments cannot be cleared.
steps.tx: **Lower pole** (lowest kidney cup) stones clear poorly after shock waves because fragments must float against gravity up a narrow neck. Clearance collapses when the **infundibular angle** (cup entry angle) drops below **30 degrees** (acute bend), the infundibulum exceeds 30 mm (long exit tunnel), or its width narrows under **5 mm** (tight throat). Send such anatomy straight to flexible ureteroscopy with a deflected laser fibre, because shock waves only scatter chips that never climb out.

rows: Poor after ESWL: send to URS

steps.say: A stent after simple ureteroscopy is optional for small stones in a pre-stented ureter. Intact lining and brief surgery need no routine splint. A stent is always placed after dilatation or sheath use. Visible grazes to the lining are also drained. Swelling and clots can block the healing ureter overnight. Remove temporary stents within two weeks to prevent crusting and infection.
steps.tx: A **ureteral stent** (internal drainage tube) after uncomplicated **ureteroscopy** (telescope stone surgery) is discretionary for small pre-stented stones with an intact urothelium. Always stent after **ureteral dilatation** (stretching a tight segment), **access sheath** use (instrument strain), or visible mucosal injury, because oedema and clots obstruct the healing ureter overnight. Remove routine stents within one to two weeks to avoid encrustation, flank pain, and urinary infection that forgotten stents invite.
